questions.question: What is SQL injection and how does it work?
questions.title: SQL Injection Attack — How It Works
questions.direct_answer: **SQL injection** is when attacker-controlled input is **concatenated into a SQL string**, so the input becomes executable SQL instead of data. Classic example: typing `' OR '1'='1` into a login bypasses the password check. It works because the query and the data are mixed into one string the DB then parses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand injection is string-concatenated input becoming SQL.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Building queries by concatenating user input with + .
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the ' OR '1'='1 payload and name parameterized queries as the fix.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **SQL injection** = user input concatenated into SQL becomes executable.
- **Root cause**: mixing code (SQL) and data (input) in one string.
- **Classic payload**: `' OR '1'='1` bypasses a login.
- **Impact**: read, modify, or destroy data.
- **Fix**: parameterized queries (`PreparedStatement`).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: SQL injection is an attack that happens when user-supplied input is concatenated directly into a SQL statement, which lets an attacker change what the query actually does. The root cause is that you're mixing two different things, the SQL code and the user's data, into a single string, and then handing that whole string to the database to parse. So if the input contains SQL syntax, the database can't tell it's supposed to be data and executes it as code. The textbook example is a login form. Suppose the query is select star from users where name equals quote, plus the username, plus quote. If the attacker types apostrophe OR apostrophe one equals apostrophe one, the where clause becomes a condition that is always true, so it returns all users and bypasses authentication entirely. And it gets worse: attackers can read data from other tables, dump sensitive information, or even destroy data with something like semicolon DROP TABLE users. The damage isn't limited to logins; any query built by concatenation, like a search box or a sort parameter, is vulnerable. The fix is to use parameterized queries, which in JDBC means a PreparedStatement with question-mark placeholders and setString. With that, the driver sends the SQL and the data to the database separately, so the input is always treated as a literal value and can never become executable SQL.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**Second-order (stored) SQL injection** is when a malicious payload is safely **stored** first, then later **read back and concatenated** into a query that runs it.

Unlike first-order (input used immediately), the attack triggers on a *later* request — so even validated-on-input data is dangerous if you trust it and concatenate it later.

**SQL injection** is when attacker-controlled input is **concatenated into a SQL string**, so the input becomes executable SQL instead of data. Classic example: typing `' OR '1'='1` into a login bypasses the password check. It works because the query and the data are mixed into one string the DB then parses.

sections.content:

sections.title: Vulnerable: input concatenated into SQL
Safe: parameterized query keeps input as data
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **String-concatenating input** into SQL with `+` — the core vulnerability.
- **Trusting client-side validation**: attackers bypass it; validate/parameterize server-side.
- **Escaping manually**: error-prone — use `PreparedStatement` instead.
- **Thinking only logins are at risk**: any concatenated query (search, sort) is vulnerable.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app connecting to a MySQL database with JDBC to query an orders table
speakable_v2.hook: Type a bit of SQL into a login box and watch it run as code. That's SQL injection in one line.

beats.text: SQL injection happens when user input gets glued straight into a SQL string. It's no longer just data. It becomes part of the SQL the database runs. So a crafted value can quietly change what the query does.
It exists because code often trusts user input as safe text. When you build a query by adding input with a plus sign, you're letting the user help write your SQL. Attackers take that offer.

items: Login bypass: a value that's always true makes the WHERE clause match every row, so anyone gets in.
Data theft: a tacked-on query can pull rows from other tables.
Data loss: a tacked-on command can wipe a whole table in one request.

beats.text: Picture a login query that pastes the username right into the SQL. An attacker types a value that ends the quote and adds an always-true test. Now the WHERE clause matches every user. Here's the non-obvious part. The database can't tell your SQL from their input. It just runs the whole string.

items: It's not just logins. Any query built with input is at risk, even a search box.
Hand-written escaping is fragile. Every database has edge cases that slip through.
Being on the OWASP list doesn't make it rare. It's still one of the most common attacks.

speakable_v2.cap: So the rule is simple. Never glue input into SQL. Use placeholders and let the driver keep data as data.
